planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root or container trees in late winter (December–February in zone 8–9); Fan-Stil needs only about 150–300 chill hours and is self-fruitful, though fruit set improves with a second pear such as LeConte or Kieffer blooming nearby. Choose an open, full-sun site with good air drainage to limit fire blight pressure.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Fan-Stil was bred by Fanick Nursery of San Antonio as an improvement on the old LeConte pear, keeping LeConte's low chill requirement (roughly 150–300 hours) while adding markedly stronger fire blight resistance, a major advantage in the humid Gulf Coast growing season. The semi-dwarf, upright tree tops out around 10–15 feet, making it a good fit for smaller home orchards, and it bears bell-shaped, pale yellow fruit blushed red that ripens in late August to September. Unlike many hybrid pears, Fan-Stil is self-fruitful and will set a crop on its own, though yields increase with a nearby cross-pollinator. Watch new growth for fire blight strikes after wet spring weather and prune out any infected shoots well below the visible damage.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Texas Fruit and Nut Production: Pears

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant; Daisui Li carries a moderate chill requirement typical of Pyrus pyrifolia cultivars, in the neighborhood of 400–500 hours, well within reach of most zone 8–9 winters. It is not self-fertile, so plant a second Asian pear such as Shinseiki, Hosui, or Shinko within about 50 feet for pollination.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Daisui Li was bred at UC Davis by Ben T. Iwakiri from a cross of the Japanese Kikusui and Chinese Tse Li pears and patented in the mid-1980s, combining Asian pear crispness with unusually large fruit size. Individual fruits can approach a pound apiece, with juicy, sweet, yellowish-green flesh, and the tree ripens its crop in mid-to-late September, after Bartlett and Shinko have finished. The tree shows good resistance to fire blight, an important trait for Gulf Coast gardens where humid spring weather favors the disease, but it requires cross-pollination from a different Asian pear cultivar to fruit well. Thin developing fruit clusters to one pear each so the tree can support the variety's characteristically oversized crop.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension — Asian Pear Variety Guide

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant; Atago needs a moderate chill accumulation, in the range of 400–500 hours common to Japanese Asian pear cultivars, which most zone 8–9 winters supply. It is not self-fertile — plant with another Pyrus pyrifolia cultivar such as Hosui or Shinko within 50 feet for reliable pollination.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Atago is a Japanese heirloom Asian pear prized for producing some of the largest fruit of any pear cultivar, commonly reaching a pound or more with light tan, lightly russeted skin and crisp, very juicy flesh. It is a late-season variety, ripening from late September into October, well after most other Asian pears have finished, and unlike some heat-loving Asian pear cultivars it develops good sweetness even where summers run cooler. Atago is not self-fruitful and needs cross-pollination from a different Asian pear cultivar blooming at the same time to set a full crop. The upright, spreading tree is a vigorous, heavy producer, so thin young fruit to prevent limb breakage under the weight of a full crop.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension — Asian Pear Variety Guide

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant; Shin Li needs a moderate chill accumulation of roughly 400–500 hours, typical of Pyrus pyrifolia cultivars and generally achievable across zone 8–9. It is not self-fertile, so plant with another Asian pear such as Shinseiki, Chojuro, or Hosui within about 50 feet for cross-pollination.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Shin Li is a patented Asian pear bred from a cross of Kikusui and Tsu Li, producing medium-to-large, round-oblate fruit with smooth yellowish-green skin flecked with russet and firm, extremely juicy white flesh carrying a distinctive sweet, spicy, faintly cinnamon-like aroma. The tree grows notably more vigorously than many other Asian pear cultivars and has performed reliably even in heavy clay soils in zone 8 trial orchards, ripening a heavy crop in mid-to-late September. Cross-pollination from a different Asian pear cultivar is required, since Shin Li will not set a good crop on its own. Keep an eye out for fire blight strikes during humid spring bloom and remove infected wood promptly, cutting well below any visible discoloration.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Texas Fruit and Nut Production: Pears

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant; Yoinashi carries a moderate chill requirement in the 400–450 hour range typical of Japanese Asian pear cultivars, well within reach of most zone 8–9 winters. It is one of the few self-pollinating Asian pears, so a single tree can bear fruit, though a second early-blooming Asian pear nearby will noticeably increase the crop.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Yoinashi (Japanese for 'good pear') is a compact, rounded Asian pear reaching only 8–15 feet at maturity, making it one of the more manageable choices for a smaller Gulf Coast home orchard. The medium-sized fruit has lightly russeted gold-to-bronze skin and crisp, aromatic flesh with butterscotch and floral notes, ripening from mid-August into September and storing several months longer than many other Asian pear cultivars. Its early bloom period and good fire blight resistance are both useful traits in the humid South, though a late freeze during an unusually early bloom year can still reduce fruit set. Because it is self-fruitful, a single tree will produce a crop, but pairing it with another early-flowering Asian pear improves yields further.
